title: Mi barrio
blurbEn: Ana describes where she lives. Watch how 'hay' introduces things you did not know were there, while 'está' places something you already know about.
body:
Vivo en un barrio pequeño, cerca de la universidad.

En mi calle hay muchas tiendas. Hay un supermercado y un banco.

Al lado de mi casa hay una plaza muy bonita. Por la tarde hay mucha gente en la plaza. Los niños juegan y las personas hablan.

El parque está lejos, pero me gusta caminar. Cada domingo camino al parque con mi hermana.
translationEn:
I live in a small neighbourhood, near the university.

On my street there are many shops. There is a supermarket and a bank.

Next to my house there is a very pretty square. In the afternoon there are a lot of people in the square. The children play and people talk.

The park is far away, but I like walking. Every Sunday I walk to the park with my sister.

hay.note: Introduces something new. Notice it is followed by 'un', 'una' or 'muchas' — never by 'el' or 'la'.

está.note: Used here because you already know which park is meant. 'Hay un parque' would be introducing one for the first time.

phrases.note: Literally 'at the side of'. Most Spanish position words end in 'de'.
